Name: information_burst_reasoning
Title: Bits Per Step: Do Information-Density Bursts Cause LLM Reasoning Failures, and Can Pacing Them Fix It?
Short Hypothesis: LLM reasoning failures are causally linked to information-density bursts — individual reasoning steps that try to transmit too many bits at once (violating local Uniform Information Density) — rather than merely being correlated with them; a locatable internal 'information-pacing' signal governs how many bits a step emits, and causally reducing bursts at high-risk steps (by inducing the model to decompose them into more, lower-density steps) improves reasoning more than length-matched extra computation. We hold a strict claim hierarchy: the PRIMARY claim is causality (bursts cause failure), the internal information-pacing locus is SECONDARY, and steering the pacing signal is TERTIARY; the proposal stands on the causal claim even if the locus or steering claims are weak.
Related Work: The Uniform Information Density (UID) hypothesis (Jaeger 2008; Genzel & Charniak 2001) posits humans pace information evenly. Recent LLM work (Gwak, Son & Kim, ACL 2025; 'Revisiting UID in LLM Reasoning Traces', 2025) computes entropy-based stepwise information-density metrics and finds a robust pattern: correct reasoning is locally uniform (smooth step-to-step transitions) but globally non-uniform, and that information-density spikes/bursts predict incorrect traces — they use this as a trace-SELECTION signal (reranking many samples). Entropy-rate work (Revisiting Entropy Rate Constancy, 2023; Constant Conditional Entropy, 2013) studies text-level uniformity but not reasoning. Crucially, ALL existing LLM-UID work is (1) purely correlational — it selects among traces the model already produced but never intervenes to change pacing, (2) treats information density as a passive readout with no internal locus, and (3) offers no causal test that bursts CAUSE failure rather than co-occur with hard steps. My prior proposals covered linguistic relativity, cognitive-analogy transfers, tokenization granularity, and difficulty-gated language-agnostic steering — none address information-density pacing, bursts, or a bits-per-step controller. We uniquely (a) causally test whether an induced information burst at a step degrades reasoning and whether burst-reduction repairs it, (b) locate an internal information-pacing signal, and (c) turn UID from a reranking heuristic into a training-free, single-pass pacing intervention, with a high-stakes clinical instance. Closest baseline family, delta in one sentence: Gwak, Son & Kim (ACL 2025) and 'Revisiting UID in LLM Reasoning Traces' (2025) use stepwise information density as a PASSIVE trace-SELECTION signal that reranks many sampled traces, whereas we convert that same signal into a single-pass CAUSAL intervention with an internal locus and a steerable controller. What would be genuinely new if true: that bursts CAUSE rather than merely flag failure and that single-pass pacing beats cost-matched reranking; if instead the causal (Experiment 1) and placement (Experiment 3) contrasts fall in the indecision band, we would have shown only a stronger version of UID reranking, and we say so explicitly.
Abstract: A striking recent finding is that an LLM's step-by-step reasoning is locally smooth but globally uneven in information density, and that sharp information-density bursts — steps that pack many bits into few tokens — reliably flag incorrect reasoning. Existing work exploits this only correlationally, as a signal for reranking many sampled traces. We ask the causal question: do information bursts CAUSE reasoning failures, and can pacing them fix reasoning in a single pass? We propose that each reasoning step has a controllable information budget, that overloading a step (a burst) is a proximal cause of downstream errors, and that an LLM carries a locatable internal 'information-pacing' signal governing how many bits it commits per step. We test three claims. First, bursts are causal, not incidental: experimentally inducing a burst (forcing the model to compress a multi-inference step into one dense token span) raises error rates beyond matched-difficulty controls, and correct traces avoid bursts at genuinely hard steps. Second, pacing is a locatable internal quantity: a probe reads a step's committed information load from hidden states before the step completes, predicting impending bursts and errors. Third, pacing is a steerable, useful lever: at high-risk (predicted-burst) steps only, we causally reduce density by inducing decomposition into more, lower-density steps, and show this Burst-Aware Pacing improves accuracy more than length-matched extra reasoning, blanket 'think more' prompting, or random-step decomposition. We evaluate on math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical-reasoning instance where a single overloaded inference step silently produces a wrong diagnosis. Our work reframes information density from a passive reranking signal into a causal, controllable resource for machine reasoning. We report the contributions as a strict hierarchy (primary: causality, Experiment 1; secondary: internal locus, Experiment 2; tertiary: steering, Experiment 5) and do not overclaim them equally. Beyond accuracy we add application-facing metrics: calibration (expected calibration error) and, in the clinical instance, confident-error severity, because the concrete payoff is a training-free, single-pass inference-time knob. If bursts are causal, inference-time prompting, best-of-N reranking, and safety monitoring should pace or flag high-density steps rather than blanket 'think more'; if bursts are non-causal, the field should abandon burst-based control and treat UID strictly as a passive reranking correlate.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights (logistic or ridge regression on frozen hidden states). Decoding is greedy for the primary condition and temperature 0.7 for any sampled condition, each sampled/steered run repeated over seeds 0, 1, 2. All effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) over 1000 item-level resamples, and behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts for model and item, written (1|model)+(1|item). Reasoning traces are segmented into steps at sentence/newline boundaries; per-step information density is mean token surprisal under the generating model plus a bits-per-inference measure normalized by content tokens, following the stepwise Uniform-Information-Density metrics of Gwak et al. 2025; a burst is a step whose density exceeds that item's within-trace running-median density by more than 1.5 standard deviations.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Bursts causally degrade reasoning rather than merely co-occurring with hard steps): Tests whether a forced information-density burst at a step raises error beyond what step difficulty alone predicts. Data: 500 items sampled from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 500 from the MATH test split (5,000 available) stratified across difficulty levels 1-5, 400 synthetic deductive-logic chains we construct (modus-ponens chaining templates, branching depth 2-6, answers auto-checkable), and 400 questions sampled from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 1,800 items total; these sizes give a few hundred items per task for stable step-level mixed-effects estimates across five models while staying within a single-GPU-week budget. On items each model first solves correctly under free reasoning, four systems are compared: (i) free baseline; (ii) burst-injection -- re-prompt with a structural constraint forcing one target multi-inference step to be compressed into a single dense token span, total reasoning content held constant; (iii) length-matched control -- add equal token count elsewhere without compressing the target step; (iv) decomposition control -- expand the same step into more, lower-density steps. Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy of burst-injection minus the length-matched control at genuinely hard steps (top difficulty tercile), from mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ condition * step_difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary metric: error-localization rate (fraction of induced errors whose first wrong step is the injected step or its direct consequence). Convincing result: burst-injection is at least 5 percentage points below the length-matched control with a CI excluding 0, at least 60% of induced errors localize to the injected step, and the decomposition control sits at or above free baseline. Indecision band: a burst-minus-length-matched gap within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) is uninformative -- compression is not separable from added content at our power, and we report that rather than a causal claim. Negative result: if burst-injection does not fall below the length-matched control (gap <= 0), bursts are not a distinct causal factor beyond difficulty and length, and H1's causal claim collapses to the prior correlational finding; only injection-compliant trials (verified content preservation) are analyzed.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- A locatable pre-emission information-pacing signal): Tests whether hidden states at a step boundary, before the step's content is emitted, encode the impending step's information load. Data: reuse the traces from Experiment 1, split 70/30 by item into probe-train and held-out sets. At each step-boundary position we extract residual-stream activations at every layer and train (only the probe is trainable) a ridge regressor to predict the impending step's density and a logistic probe to predict whether it will be a burst, reporting per-layer held-out AUROC and R-squared; baselines are boundary token-entropy, post-hoc per-step surprisal, and verbalized confidence elicited from the model. Decisive metric first: held-out burst-prediction AUROC from pre-step hidden states; secondary: Spearman correlation between an item's mean pre-step burst probability and final-answer error. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70 on held-out items, exceeding the best baseline by >= 0.05, with pre-step burst probability predicting item error at Spearman rho >= 0.2 (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: AUROC in 0.55-0.65 is a weak signal we cannot separate from generic entropy, and we would decline to claim a dedicated pacing readout. Negative result: AUROC ~ 0.5 or no gain over the entropy baseline means no locatable pre-emission pacing signal exists, refuting H2 and leaving pacing a post-hoc description.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Burst-Aware Pacing beats length-matched extra computation): Tests whether reducing density only at predicted-burst steps improves accuracy more than simply computing more. Data: the same 1,800 items. Five single-pass systems at matched token budgets: no-intervention; blanket "think step by step / think more" prompting; random-step decomposition (matched number of interventions and tokens); a Uniform-Information-Density reranking baseline (Gwak et al. 2025, cost-matched to the same token budget); and Burst-Aware Pacing -- flag high-risk steps online with the Experiment-2 pre-step probe (or a surprisal-threshold proxy) and inject a decomposition instruction only at flagged steps. Decisive metric first: accuracy at matched token budget, reported as an accuracy-versus-token-cost curve, with the primary contrast Burst-Aware Pacing minus random-step decomposition; secondary: accuracy versus blanket prompting and versus reranking at equal cost. Convincing result: Burst-Aware Pacing matches or exceeds blanket prompting and reranking at equal or lower token cost and beats random-step decomposition by >= 3 points (CI excludes 0), showing that where you pace matters, not merely that you pace. Indecision band: Burst-Aware Pacing within +/-2 points of random-step decomposition means placement is not demonstrably load-bearing though pacing may still help. Negative result: no gain over no-intervention, or a deficit versus blanket prompting at equal cost, refutes H3's usefulness claim.

Experiment 4 (H1 and H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether a single overloaded clinical inference step silently causes misdiagnosis and whether Burst-Aware Pacing mitigates it. Data: 300 differential-diagnosis vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) fine-distinction items plus constructed vignettes in which multiple clinical inferences can be compressed into one dense assertion; we use 300 because expert spot-checking of ground truth is costly and 300 supports the paired burst/pace contrasts. Systems: free baseline, burst-injection at the pivotal clinical step, and Burst-Aware Pacing. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate (wrong diagnosis emitted with high stated confidence); secondary: overall diagnostic accuracy. Convincing result: burst-injection raises confident misdiagnosis and Burst-Aware Pacing lowers it by >= 5 points on fine-distinction cases (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: a pacing effect within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no movement means the pacing lever does not transfer to high-stakes reasoning, bounding the claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 5 (H2 and H3 -- Causal pacing-direction steering, mechanistic depth): Tests whether directly lowering the internal pacing signal reproduces the Burst-Aware Pacing benefit without any decomposition prompt. Data: the 1,800 items from Experiment 1. We derive a difference-in-means "pacing" direction from high-density-minus-low-density step-boundary activation contrasts (matched content) at the best probe layer, then steer minus-direction at flagged steps; controls are random-direction steering of matched norm and no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy gain of minus-direction steering over random-direction steering, with a dose-response sweep over steering magnitude; secondary: specificity (accuracy change on easy items, which must stay within 1 point, and fluency by perplexity). Convincing result: a monotonic dose-response and a >= 3-point accuracy gain over random-direction steering with preserved easy-item accuracy. Indecision band: a gain within +/-2 points of random-direction steering leaves the direction unproven, in which case the prompt-based Burst-Aware Pacing and the burst-injection causal result stand independently. Negative result: no benefit from a clean direction, or benefit indistinguishable from random steering, means the internal pacing quantity is not a usable causal lever even if it is readable.

Experiment 6 (Pre-registered identification and robustness ablations): We pre-register the causal identification strategy before running: the decisive contrast is burst-injection minus the length-matched control at genuinely hard steps, with a semantic-preservation check (content-preservation verified by entailment both ways plus exact preservation of required operations) as an inclusion gate. We report the exact fraction of burst-injection trials excluded for non-compliance and run a sensitivity analysis that re-includes excluded trials under worst-case labels to bound selection bias. Ablations: (a) burst threshold swept over 1.0/1.5/2.0 within-trace SD and a median-absolute-deviation variant; (b) segmentation over sentence, newline, and clause boundaries; (c) alternative density definitions (mean token surprisal, bits-per-inference normalized by content tokens, and a local entropy-rate estimate). For the Experiment-2 probe we add explicit controls regressing out step difficulty, verbalized confidence, and step length, report probe calibration (ECE), and test cross-task and held-out-model (out-of-distribution) generalization of the burst probe. Convincing result: the sign and rough magnitude of the causal and diagnostic effects are stable across thresholds, segmentations, and density definitions, and the probe retains its edge after difficulty/confidence/length controls and under OOD transfer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Surprisal-based information density is model-internal and confounded with step difficulty — hard steps are naturally denser; mitigated by matched-difficulty controls, by testing the burst-injection vs length-matched vs decomposition CONTROLS (isolating compression from content/length), and by error-localization checks that show the injected step specifically drives failure. (2) Burst injection via prompting may be non-compliant or change content, not just density; we verify compliance, hold reasoning content constant, and analyze only compliant trials. (3) The pacing probe may capture generic difficulty/confidence rather than a genuine bits-per-step controller; mitigated by held-out validation, comparison to confidence/entropy baselines, the pre-step (before-emission) prediction requirement, and random-direction steering controls. (4) BAP's decomposition prompt could help simply by adding tokens/'thinking time'; the random-step-decomposition and cost-matched reranking baselines isolate the value of WHERE pacing is applied. (5) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (6) Global-non-uniformity findings (Gwak et al.) suggest LLM reasoning legitimately needs some bursts; our claim is specifically about bursts at HARD/pivotal steps, and a null result (bursts are benign or even helpful) would itself be informative, refining when UID applies to machine reasoning. (7) The optional steering variant depends on a clean pacing direction; if unavailable, the prompt-based BAP and the causal burst-injection results stand independently. (8) The UID framing is operationalized information-theoretically and behaviorally, not as a claim of human-like production planning. (9) Negative-result value: a clean null (bursts non-causal, or pacing no better than length-matched compute) is decision-relevant, not a failed study -- it would tell the community to stop pursuing burst/UID-based test-time control knobs and to treat information density strictly as a passive reranking correlate.
